title: Graphs: Alien Dictionary
oneLiner: Recover an unknown alphabet from a sorted word list: each adjacent pair of words gives one letter-before-letter rule, and a topological sort of those rules is the alphabet.
keyTakeaway: Compare each pair of neighbouring words: the first position where they differ says letter a comes before letter b, an edge a -> b. Everything else about the pair says nothing. Topologically sort the letters (Kahn's algorithm); a cycle, or a word followed by its own prefix, means no valid order exists.
explanation:
An alien language uses lowercase English letters in an unknown order. You are given its dictionary, a list of words sorted in that order. Return a string of all the letters that appear, in an order consistent with the dictionary, or "" if no order is possible. When several orders are possible, this exercise asks for one specific one: whenever more than one letter is free to come next, take the alphabetically smallest (a min-heap, or a sorted set, as the ready pool). For ["wrt", "wrf", "er", "ett", "rftt"] the answer is "wertf".

Step 1, extract rules. Sorted order means each word compares less than or equal to the next. For one adjacent pair, scan to the first position where the letters differ: that pair of letters is the only thing the comparison tells you ("wrt" before "wrf" means t before f). Later positions tell you nothing. Only adjacent pairs matter; non-adjacent ones follow from them.

One special case: if no position differs and the first word is longer, as in ["abc", "ab"], the list cannot be sorted in any alphabet (a prefix always comes first), so return "".

Step 2, order the letters. Letters are nodes, rules are edges a -> b, and you need an order with every edge pointing forwards: a topological sort, as in Topological Sort and Course Schedule. Count each letter's in-degree, start with the letters that have none, repeatedly output the smallest ready letter and decrement its successors. If fewer letters come out than exist, the rules contain a cycle (like z before x and x before z) and the answer is "". Remember to include letters that appear in no rule at all.

Building the rules reads every character once, O(C) for C total characters. The sort is over at most 26 letters and their edges, so it is tiny; with the heap it is O(U log U + E) for U distinct letters. Overall O(C).

The visualization runs ["wrt", "wrf", "er", "ett", "rftt"].

visualizationSteps.message: Words in alien sorted order. Each adjacent pair can reveal one rule: its first differing letters.
"wrt" before "wrf": first difference at index 2, so t comes before f. Rules so far: t<f.
"wrf" before "er": first difference at index 0, so w comes before e. Rules so far: t<f, w<e.
"er" before "ett": first difference at index 1, so r comes before t. Rules so far: t<f, w<e, r<t.
"ett" before "rftt": first difference at index 0, so e comes before r. Rules so far: t<f, w<e, r<t, e<r.
Output w, the smallest letter with no unplaced predecessor. Its successors lose one in-degree; ready now: [e].
Output e, the smallest letter with no unplaced predecessor. Its successors lose one in-degree; ready now: [r].
Output r, the smallest letter with no unplaced predecessor. Its successors lose one in-degree; ready now: [t].
Output t, the smallest letter with no unplaced predecessor. Its successors lose one in-degree; ready now: [f].
Output f, the smallest letter with no unplaced predecessor. Its successors lose one in-degree; ready now: [].
All 5 letters placed, so there was no cycle: "wertf".

recognitionSignals: An unknown ordering must be inferred from examples that are already sorted.
Pairwise "comes before" facts and you need one total order, or to detect that none exists: topological sort.
gotchas: Only the FIRST differing character of an adjacent pair is a rule; stop scanning after it.
A word followed by its own prefix (["abc", "ab"]) is invalid even though no letters differ.
Letters that appear in no rule must still be in the answer.
Adding the same edge twice inflates the in-degree; keep edges in a set.
confusableWith: Topological Sort and Course Schedule hand you the edges; here deriving the edges from the words is half the problem.
Sorting words with a custom comparator (Verifying an Alien Dictionary) goes the other way: the alphabet is given and you check the list.

complexity.note: Here L is the total number of characters in all the words: building the rules reads each character at most once. The graph has at most 26 letters and 26 · 25 edges, so the topological sort and all the maps are bounded by a constant.
